observation_summary: The compiler incorrectly reports a lower percentage of typed code when encountering object literal keys within enums, causing tests to fail because they expect 100% typing.
hypothesis: The type-checking logic incorrectly attempts to validate the type of object literal keys, which are not inherently typeable in this context. The fix involves adding a check to identify object literal keys and explicitly marking them as non-typeable, preventing them from being counted as untyped.
prediction: The code will now check if a node is an object literal key. If it is, it will set a flag (typeable = false) to exclude it from the typing percentage calculation, rather than incorrectly flagging it as untyped.
experiment_rationale: The fix diff shows the addition of an 'else' block to an existing conditional check (`!NodeUtil.isObjectLitKey`). This block sets `typeable = false` when the node is an object literal key, confirming that the root cause was an incorrect validation/counting logic for these specific nodes.
reasoning_summary: The bug is a classic case of incorrect validation logic. The compiler was attempting to enforce a type check on nodes (object literal keys) that should not be subject to that check. By adding a guard (the 'else' block) to correctly identify and exclude these nodes from the typing tally, the issue is resolved. This fits the 'Checking' category perfectly as it involves correcting the conditional logic that determines whether a node is considered 'typeable'.
evidence_used: The fix diff shows an added 'else' block to 'if (!NodeUtil.isObjectLitKey(n, n.getParent()))'.
The fix sets 'typeable = false' inside this new block.
The bug report mentions that the name string nodes in enums have no type and should not be counted in the % type tally.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix modifies the logic, it is specifically a correction to a conditional check (a guard) that determines whether a node is counted, rather than a rewrite of a computational algorithm.
